course.title: English Literature & Composition
course.description: English Literature and Composition teaches you to read poems, plays, and novels closely and to write disciplined analytical essays about them. Every text studied here is a public-domain work you can read in full for free through Project Gutenberg, from Shakespeare and Austen to Dickens, the Brontes, Shelley, Poe, Whitman, and Dickinson. The course follows the shape of an AP English Literature and Composition syllabus, moving from close reading through the finished, revised essay.

questions.prompt: A simile differs from a metaphor because a simile...
options: states outright that one thing is another
questions.explanation: A simile signals its comparison with 'like' or 'as' ('cheeks like roses'); a metaphor asserts the identity directly ('her cheeks were roses').

questions.prompt: A story told by an 'I' who takes part in the events uses which point of view?
questions.explanation: First-person narration speaks as 'I' from inside the action, so we see only what that narrator knows and chooses to tell.

questions.prompt: In a play, a soliloquy is...
options: a speech a character makes while alone, revealing private thought
the closing scene of the drama
a song performed by the chorus
questions.explanation: A soliloquy lets a character think aloud when no one else can hear, so Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be' exposes his mind directly.

questions.prompt: A Shakespearean (English) sonnet contains how many lines?
questions.explanation: An English sonnet runs fourteen lines: three quatrains and a closing couplet, usually in iambic pentameter.

questions.prompt: The repeated vowel sound in the phrase 'fleet feet sweep' is an example of...
questions.explanation: Assonance is the repetition of a vowel sound (the long 'e' here); alliteration repeats an initial consonant instead.

questions.prompt: A strong thesis statement in a literary essay should...
options: make an arguable claim about how the text works
list every device the author uses
questions.explanation: A thesis stakes out a claim a reader could reasonably dispute, then the essay defends it with evidence from the text.

questions.prompt: Dickens opens A Tale of Two Cities with 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.' This balancing of opposites is...
questions.explanation: Antithesis sets contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical form, sharpening each against the other.

questions.prompt: The writer's emotional attitude toward the subject of a work is its...
questions.explanation: Tone is the attitude the language conveys toward the subject or reader; it is built from diction, imagery, and rhythm.

lessons.title: Reading closely: how to analyze a text
lessons.grammar_note: Write about literature in the present tense: Austen 'writes,' Hamlet 'hesitates.' The literary present treats the text as always happening on the page.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to slow a passage down and read it the way an analyst does, noticing not only what a sentence says but how its word choice, rhythm, and structure make meaning. You will learn to move from observation ('the sentence is very long') to interpretation ('the length mimics the character's runaway anxiety'), which is the heart of every literary essay you will write in this course. Warm-up: think of the last book that stayed with you. Was it the plot you remembered, or a particular voice, image, or sentence? That lingering detail is usually where close reading begins, because the parts a text lingers on are the parts it wants you to weigh. Analysis is simply paying deliberate attention to those parts and asking why the writer made the choices they did, rather than reading only to find out what happens next.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Close reading means treating a short passage as evidence and asking how its small choices produce its large effects. You look at diction (which words, and why those and not their synonyms), syntax (how sentences are built, where they pause or rush), imagery (what the words make you see, hear, or feel), and tone (the attitude the language carries). A useful habit is to separate three layers: what the text literally says, what it implies, and how it makes you feel it. Observation comes first, interpretation second, and your interpretation must point back to specific words on the page. Never settle for 'this shows the theme of love.' Ask which words, arranged how, create that impression, and what a reader gains by noticing it. The goal is not to decode a hidden message the author buried but to account for the experience the language actually creates.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Jane Eyre opens: 'There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.' Read it slowly. The flat, negative construction ('no possibility') begins the novel in refusal and limitation, not action. There is no 'I' yet, no name, only a blank, impersonal statement about the weather and the day, which quietly tells us this is a narrator used to being denied things. The word 'possibility' hints at a mind that notices what it cannot do. Charlotte Bronte could have written 'It rained hard all morning,' but that would report weather; her sentence reports constraint. From one line we can already argue a claim: the novel announces its central tension, a watchful self hemmed in by circumstance, in its opening grammar. That is close reading. We moved from a plain observation about word choice to an interpretation, and every step stayed anchored to the actual words Bronte chose.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Close-read Austen's first sentence of Pride and Prejudice: 'It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.' Answer these: 1) Which words sound grand and formal? 2) Is the statement actually a universal truth? 3) What is the effect of that gap? Model answers: 1) 'truth universally acknowledged,' 'in possession of,' and 'must be in want of' borrow the weight of philosophy or law. 2) No; it is a piece of local marriage-market gossip dressed as a law of nature. 3) The mismatch between the grand phrasing and the trivial claim creates irony, and that ironic voice, mocking its own society even as it describes it, is the governing tone of the whole novel. Notice how a single sentence previews a book's attitude.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: summarizing the plot instead of analyzing the language, so your paragraph tells what happens but never why the words matter. Mistake: naming a device ('this is a metaphor') and stopping, without saying what the device does. Always push to the 'so what.' Mistake: writing 'I feel' without pointing to the words that caused the feeling. Exit ticket: (a) What three layers should you separate when you close-read a passage? (b) Why is 'this shows the theme of fear' an incomplete claim? Answers: (a) what the text literally says, what it implies, and how it makes you feel it. (b) It names a theme but never shows which words, arranged how, create the fear, so there is no evidence and no interpretation, only a label.

lessons.title: The elements of fiction
lessons.grammar_note: Keep character and author separate: the narrator of Jane Eyre is Jane, a created voice, not Charlotte Bronte. Confusing the two muddles your analysis.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to name and use the five building blocks that fiction is made from: plot, character, setting, point of view, and theme. More importantly, you will learn to connect them, because a well-written story never treats these as separate parts. A setting shapes the characters who live in it; a point of view decides what we can know; a plot is only the arrangement through which theme emerges. Warm-up: picture a story you know well and try to state its theme in one sentence that is not simply its topic. 'Revenge' is a topic; 'revenge consumes the avenger along with the target' is a theme, because it makes a claim. Learning to tell topics from themes is one of the most useful skills this lesson builds, and it will carry straight into your essays.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Plot is the ordered sequence of events, usually built as exposition, rising action, climax, and resolution; it is distinct from story, which is just the raw events in time. Character is the people who act: round, developing characters versus flat, static ones, revealed through what they say, do, and prompt others to feel. Setting is the time and place, and it often carries mood and meaning rather than mere backdrop. Point of view is the vantage from which we receive everything: first person ('I'), third-person limited (one character's mind), or third-person omniscient (all minds). Theme is the central insight about human life the work explores, stated as a claim, not a word. These elements interlock: change the point of view and the plot's meaning shifts, because what we are allowed to know changes.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Consider setting and point of view in Frankenstein. Shelley frames the story in letters, then nests Victor's first-person confession inside, and the creature's own account inside that. We reach the creature only through two narrators who fear and loathe him, so the structure itself makes us distrust, then slowly pity, him. Setting reinforces this: Victor assembles his creature on 'a dreary night of November,' and the cold, desolate Arctic frames the telling. The bleak settings externalize isolation, the book's great subject. From these choices we can argue a theme as a claim: Frankenstein suggests that a creator's refusal of responsibility, not the creature's nature, produces the monstrousness, and the layered narration forces us to judge Victor as carefully as we judge what he made. Notice the method: we read setting and point of view as deliberate choices, then stated the theme they build.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Using any public-domain novel you know, do the following. 1) State its plot in one sentence (events in order). 2) Name the point of view and one thing it hides from us. 3) Turn its topic into a theme-claim. Model, using Pride and Prejudice: 1) A sharp-witted young woman and a proud wealthy man misjudge each other, each changes, and they finally marry. 2) Third-person limited, mostly through Elizabeth, so we share her mistaken first reading of Darcy and cannot see his private regret until she does. 3) Topic 'pride'; theme-claim: 'first impressions, fed by pride and prejudice on both sides, blind people to the truth of others until humility corrects them.' A theme always asserts something arguable about how people or the world behave.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing topic with theme, writing 'the theme is love' instead of a claim about love. Mistake: treating setting as decoration rather than as meaning, so you never ask why the author chose that place and time. Mistake: forgetting that point of view limits knowledge; if a first-person narrator says a rival is wicked, that is the narrator's view, not a fact. Exit ticket: (a) Name the five elements of fiction. (b) Rewrite the topic 'ambition' as a theme-claim. Answers: (a) plot, character, setting, point of view, theme. (b) A sample: 'unchecked ambition isolates a person from the very people whose regard they sought,' which is arguable and points toward evidence, unlike the bare word 'ambition.'

lessons.title: Figurative language and imagery
lessons.grammar_note: Introduce a quoted image and then read it: do not drop a line and move on. The reading, not the quotation, is your analysis.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to identify the main figures of speech, metaphor, simile, personification, symbol, and imagery, and, more importantly, to explain the work each one does in its passage. Spotting a metaphor is a vocabulary exercise; explaining why the writer reached for that metaphor rather than plain statement is literary analysis. Warm-up: think of an everyday figure of speech, such as 'drowning in work.' What does 'drowning' add that 'very busy' does not? The figure smuggles in panic, helplessness, and the sense of being pulled under, feelings a literal phrase leaves out. That surplus of feeling is exactly what writers chase, and learning to put that surplus into words is the skill this lesson trains, because your essays will live or die on how well you read images.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Figurative language says one thing in terms of another to create meaning beyond the literal. A metaphor asserts an identity ('life's but a walking shadow'); a simile compares with 'like' or 'as' ('my love is like a red, red rose'); personification gives human qualities to nonhuman things ('the wind whispered'). A symbol is an object or image that carries meaning larger than itself, like a raven standing for grief that will not leave. Imagery is the broader term for language that appeals to the senses, sight, sound, touch, taste, smell, and builds the felt texture of a scene. When you analyze, ask three questions of any image: what two things are being linked, what quality transfers from one to the other, and what feeling or idea that transfer produces. The answer to the third question is your interpretation.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Take Macbeth's lines after his wife's death: 'Out, out, brief candle! Life's but a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage, and then is heard no more.' The candle is a metaphor for a human life, small, flickering, easily snuffed; 'brief' insists on how little it lasts. Then life becomes 'a walking shadow,' something insubstantial that only imitates solidity, and next 'a poor player,' an actor who performs loudly ('struts and frets') and is then silenced forever. The images pile up, each making life more empty and theatrical than the last. The transfer of qualities, from candle to shadow to actor, carries Macbeth's final conviction that existence is noisy, short, and meaningless. We did not just label metaphors; we traced what each image gives and where the sequence lands emotionally.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Read the first line of Dickinson's poem: 'Because I could not stop for Death - He kindly stopped for me.' Answer: 1) What figure of speech turns Death into a character? 2) What quality does the word 'kindly' transfer to him? 3) What unsettling effect does that create? Model answers: 1) Personification: Death is given a human action, stopping, and later drives a carriage. 2) 'Kindly' lends Death courtesy and gentleness, as if he were a polite suitor. 3) The gap between the gentle manners and the terrifying subject makes death feel calm and almost welcome, which is far more disturbing than open fear would be. Notice how one adjective, read closely, reshapes the whole tone of a poem.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: hunting for devices like a scavenger and listing them without reading any, producing a paragraph that names metaphors but interprets none. Mistake: mislabeling, calling every comparison a metaphor when a 'like' or 'as' makes it a simile. Mistake: treating a symbol as a fixed code ('the rose always means love') instead of reading what it means in this text. Exit ticket: (a) What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor? (b) When you analyze an image, what is the key third question to ask? Answers: (a) a simile compares with 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor states the identity directly. (b) What feeling or idea does the transfer of qualities from one thing to the other produce, which is where your interpretation lives.

lessons.title: Poetry: form, meter, sound, and the sonnet
lessons.grammar_note: When you quote across a line break, mark it with a slash and keep the original spelling: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? / Thou art more lovely and more temperate.'

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to read a poem as a made object, hearing its meter, catching its rhymes and sound patterns, and seeing how its form shapes its meaning. You will also learn the sonnet, the single most useful form to know well, because its structure is an argument you can follow. Warm-up: say aloud 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?' and tap the beats. You will feel five soft-loud pairs, da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM da-DUM. That steady heartbeat is iambic pentameter, the backbone of English verse, and once you can hear it you can also hear when a poet breaks it on purpose. Hearing the beat is the first step toward reading poetry as something built, not merely felt.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Poetry organizes language by line, sound, and rhythm as much as by meaning. Meter is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables; the iamb (unstressed-stressed) is the most common foot, and five iambs per line make iambic pentameter. Rhyme and sound devices, alliteration (repeated initial consonants), assonance (repeated vowels), and consonance (repeated consonants), knit lines together and draw the ear to key words. Form is the poem's shape and rules: a sonnet, for instance, is fourteen lines of iambic pentameter. The English (Shakespearean) sonnet rhymes abab cdcd efef gg and runs as three quatrains plus a couplet; often the first eight lines pose a situation and the final six, especially the couplet, turn or resolve it. Reading form means asking how the shape stages the thought.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Shakespeare's Sonnet 18 opens: 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? / Thou art more lovely and more temperate.' The first quatrain raises a comparison and immediately finds summer wanting: it is too short, too hot, too changeable ('rough winds do shake the darling buds of May'). The poem builds its problem, summer fades, beauty fades, then turns at the couplet: 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.' The turn solves the problem the quatrains posed: the beloved will not fade because the poem itself will keep them alive. Notice how the sonnet's form is the argument. The quatrains set up a worry about time, and the couplet delivers the counterclaim. Reading the structure let us see the poem as a small, complete piece of reasoning.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Scan and read Poe's opening line: 'Once upon a midnight dreary, while I pondered, weak and weary.' Answer: 1) What sound device links 'weak and weary'? 2) What sound device links 'midnight' and 'pondered' internally? 3) What mood do these repetitions build? Model answers: 1) Alliteration, the repeated 'w,' plus the internal rhyme of 'dreary' and 'weary.' 2) Internal rhyme and a heavy, chiming rhythm within the line. 3) The insistent repetition and the trudging beat create a hypnotic, exhausted gloom that matches the speaker's sleepless grief, so the sound performs the feeling before any event occurs. Reading poetry always means letting your ear do part of the analysis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: paraphrasing a poem into prose and ignoring its sound and shape, which throws away half of what a poem is. Mistake: counting feet mechanically and never asking why a poet departs from the meter at a charged moment. Mistake: assuming every fourteen-line poem is the same; the English and Italian sonnets turn in different places. Exit ticket: (a) How many lines is a sonnet, and what is its usual meter? (b) In an English sonnet, where does the thought most often turn? Answers: (a) fourteen lines, usually iambic pentameter. (b) At the final couplet (sometimes earlier, after the first eight lines), where the poem resolves or reverses the situation its quatrains set up.

questions.prompt: The ordered arrangement of events in a story, shaped as exposition, rising action, climax, and resolution, is its...
questions.explanation: Plot is the deliberate arrangement of events; theme is the insight that arrangement reveals.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a theme rather than a topic?
options: unchecked ambition isolates a person from those they love
questions.explanation: A theme makes an arguable claim about human life; the others are bare subjects.

questions.prompt: 'Life's but a walking shadow' is best described as a...
questions.explanation: It asserts an identity between life and a shadow with no 'like' or 'as,' so it is a metaphor.

questions.prompt: Iambic pentameter is a line made of...
questions.explanation: Five iambs, each an unstressed then stressed syllable, give the ten-syllable da-DUM rhythm.

questions.prompt: In Frankenstein, nesting the creature's account inside Victor's and the letters chiefly works to...
options: shape and complicate how we judge the creature
questions.explanation: The framed, second-hand narration makes us distrust, then pity, the creature, steering our judgment.

questions.prompt: The repetition of an initial consonant sound, as in 'weak and weary,' is called...
questions.explanation: Alliteration repeats initial consonants; assonance repeats vowel sounds.

lessons.title: Drama and Shakespeare: tragedy and the soliloquy
lessons.grammar_note: Cite drama by act, scene, and line when you can (Macbeth, 5.5), and quote verse with slashes at the line breaks.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to read a Shakespearean tragedy as drama rather than as a novel in disguise, attending to how meaning arrives through speech and performance, and you will learn to analyze the soliloquy, the device that gives us direct access to a character's mind. Warm-up: in a novel a narrator can tell us what a character thinks; a play has no narrator, so how does a dramatist show us a hidden thought? The answer is the soliloquy, a speech delivered alone that lets the audience overhear the mind at work. Knowing what to do with a soliloquy is the single most valuable skill for writing about Shakespeare, and it is where this lesson spends its effort, because those speeches carry a tragedy's deepest meaning.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A tragedy traces the downfall of a protagonist, often a person of stature, through a fatal flaw or error combined with circumstance, moving toward suffering and, usually, death, while asking large questions about fate, guilt, and choice. Shakespeare writes mainly in blank verse, unrhymed iambic pentameter, and raises or lowers that register to mark emotion and status. The key dramatic tools are dialogue, which reveals character through conflict; dramatic irony, where we know what a character does not; and the soliloquy, where a character alone speaks their thought aloud so we alone hear it. When you analyze a soliloquy, ask what the character is weighing, how the language stages the struggle, and how our private access changes our sympathy. The speech is action: minds change on stage in real time.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Hamlet, alone, begins: 'To be, or not to be, that is the question.' The soliloquy is a mind reasoning with itself about whether to go on living. The grammar enacts the deadlock: a bare either-or ('to be, or not to be') with no verb of decision, because Hamlet cannot decide. He weighs suffering ('the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune') against the unknown of death ('the undiscover'd country from whose bourn no traveller returns'), and it is fear of that unknown, he concludes, that makes us endure. Because we hear this in solitude, we judge Hamlet not as the hesitant prince others see but from inside his paralysis, which transforms our sympathy. The analysis is not 'Hamlet is sad'; it is an account of how the speech's structure, its balanced opposites and unanswered questions, performs a mind unable to act.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Read Macbeth's soliloquy on hearing of his wife's death: 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace from day to day, to the last syllable of recorded time.' Answer: 1) What does the triple repetition of 'tomorrow' enact? 2) What does 'creeps in this petty pace' suggest about how he now sees time? 3) What has changed in Macbeth by this point? Model answers: 1) The dull, endless repetition makes future days feel identical and meaningless, a treadmill rather than hope. 2) Time has become small ('petty') and crawling, drained of purpose. 3) The ambitious man who once seized the future now sees life as empty routine, so his tragedy is complete: he has won the crown and lost all meaning. Read the rhythm, and the despair is audible.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: paraphrasing a soliloquy into modern prose and calling that analysis, which discards the very language that carries the meaning. Mistake: treating a character's self-description as objective truth; a soliloquy is sincere but not always reliable. Mistake: forgetting the play is performed, so pace, pauses, and address to the audience are part of the meaning. Exit ticket: (a) What is a soliloquy, and why is it so valuable to the audience? (b) Why is 'Hamlet is indecisive' an incomplete reading of his first great soliloquy? Answers: (a) a speech delivered alone that lets us overhear a character's private thought directly, with no narrator. (b) It states a conclusion without showing how the speech's balanced opposites and unanswered questions perform the indecision, so it names a trait but offers no evidence or interpretation.

lessons.title: The novel: narrative technique, tone, diction, and style
lessons.grammar_note: Diction means word choice; syntax means sentence construction; style is the habitual pattern of both. Use the precise term rather than the vague 'the writing.'

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to analyze how a novel is told, its narration, and how an author's tone, diction, and style produce their distinctive voice. You will learn to describe a writer's style precisely instead of calling it 'good' or 'flowing.' Warm-up: compare 'It is a truth universally acknowledged' with 'There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.' Both open great novels, yet one is witty and worldly, the other plain and watchful. The difference is not subject but diction and syntax, the writer's choices of words and sentence shape. Learning to put that difference into exact language, naming tone and tracing diction, is the skill this lesson builds, and it is the bridge between reading fiction and writing about it in the essays still to come.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Narrative technique is how a story reaches us: the choice of narrator, the handling of time (chronological, flashback, framed), and the distance between narrator and character. Tone is the attitude the prose conveys, whether ironic, tender, bitter, or detached, and it is built, not declared. Diction is word choice, formal or plain, Latinate or Anglo-Saxon, abstract or concrete, and small shifts in diction swing tone sharply. Style is the recurring pattern of a writer's diction and syntax, their verbal fingerprint: Austen's balanced, ironic sentences, Dickens's piled-up clauses and vivid lists, Bronte's spare, watchful plainness. To analyze style, quote a representative sentence and describe its moves concretely: Is it long or short? Does it balance clauses? Which words carry the attitude? Then connect those moves to the effect they create on a reader.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Read Austen's narration of Mr. Collins: he is described, with mock gravity, as a man in whom 'the subjection in which his father had brought him up had given him originally great humility of manner; but it was now a good deal counteracted by the self-conceit of a weak head.' The style is the analysis. The sentence is balanced ('humility of manner' set against 'self-conceit of a weak head'), the diction is elevated and abstract, and that formal, measured phrasing is exactly what makes the demolition so funny: Austen dismantles Mr. Collins in the calm, judicious tone of someone stating a settled fact. The irony lives in the gap between the dignified sentence and the foolish man it describes. To call this merely 'descriptive' would miss everything; naming the balance, the diction, and the ironic tone shows how the voice itself passes judgment.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Analyze the style of Dickens's opening of A Tale of Two Cities: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness.' Answer: 1) What sentence pattern repeats? 2) What figure of speech governs each pair? 3) What is the effect of the accumulation? Model answers: 1) A repeated parallel structure, 'it was the ___ of ___,' hammered again and again (anaphora). 2) Antithesis: each clause yokes an opposite to its partner ('best' against 'worst'). 3) The piling of contradictions makes the age feel vast, divided, and contradictory, and the drumbeat of parallel clauses gives the prose an oratorical sweep. Naming the pattern, the figure, and the effect is a full style analysis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: describing style with empty praise ('beautiful,' 'engaging') instead of naming concrete features of diction and syntax. Mistake: confusing tone with mood; tone is the author's attitude, mood is the feeling created in the reader, though they are related. Mistake: ignoring the narrator, treating a first-person judgment as the novel's own verdict. Exit ticket: (a) Define diction, syntax, and style, and say how they relate. (b) Why is 'Austen's writing is elegant' a weak critical claim? Answers: (a) diction is word choice, syntax is sentence construction, and style is the habitual pattern of both. (b) It praises without evidence; a strong claim would name a specific feature, such as her balanced, ironic sentences, and show what that feature does to the reader.

lessons.title: Building a literary argument: thesis, claims, and evidence

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to turn your close reading into an argument: a debatable thesis, supporting claims, and evidence quoted and embedded so smoothly that quotation and analysis read as one. This is the move from noticing things about a text to persuading a reader of an interpretation, and it is the core of every analytical essay you will write. Warm-up: which of these could a reasonable reader disagree with? (a) 'Hamlet contains several soliloquies.' (b) 'Hamlet's soliloquies dramatize a mind that reasons itself out of action.' The first is a fact; the second is a claim, and only claims can anchor an essay. A thesis must be arguable, specific, and supportable from the text, and building one is the task this lesson trains, because an essay is only as strong as the claim it defends.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A literary argument has three parts working together. The thesis is your central arguable claim about how the text works and why it matters, stated in one or two sentences near the start. Supporting claims are the smaller arguments, usually one per body paragraph, that together prove the thesis; each should be a sentence you could defend, not a plot summary. Evidence is specific quotation and detail from the text, and it must be embedded, woven into your own sentence with a frame and immediately followed by analysis, never dropped alone as a line of its own. The reliable paragraph shape is claim, then evidence, then analysis that ties the evidence back to the claim and the claim back to the thesis. Evidence never speaks for itself; your reading of it is the argument.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Here is a model body paragraph you can imitate. Claim: Shelley makes the creature's eloquence, not his appearance, the source of our sympathy. Embedded evidence and analysis: When the creature finally speaks, he insists, 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend,' a sentence whose balanced grammar sets an original goodness against a later, caused ruin. The phrasing matters: 'made me' places the cause outside himself, so the line argues that cruelty, not nature, produced his violence. By granting the creature a voice this articulate, Shelley forces the reader to weigh his reasoning rather than recoil at his face, which supports the essay's larger claim that the novel locates monstrousness in neglect rather than in the body. Notice the shape: the claim comes first, the quotation is folded into a sentence of mine, and the analysis reads the exact words and then links back to the thesis. Study that quotation handling; it is the model your own paragraphs should follow.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Your task: write one body paragraph (about 6 to 9 sentences) arguing a single claim about a public-domain text you know, using the claim-evidence-analysis shape and at least one embedded quotation. Choose a focused claim, not a theme-word. A model to measure yourself against, on Pride and Prejudice: 'Austen uses Elizabeth's wit as a form of self-protection. When she tells Darcy she hopes 'never to ridicule what is wise or good,' the careful qualification shows a mind defending its own judgment even while appearing to concede, so her jokes are not mere charm but armor against a world that would marry her off cheaply. This supports the view that the novel treats irony as a woman's scarce instrument of power.' Match that structure: claim, embedded quotation, reading, link to a larger point.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: a thesis that states a fact or a topic rather than an arguable claim. Mistake: the 'dropped quotation,' a line of text given its own sentence with no frame and no reading after it. Mistake: quoting at length and then paraphrasing instead of analyzing the specific words. Self-check rubric, mark yes to each: my thesis is a claim a reasonable reader could dispute; each body paragraph makes one defensible claim; every quotation is embedded in my own sentence; analysis follows each quotation and reads specific words; each paragraph links back to the thesis. Exit ticket: rewrite 'There is a lot of nature imagery in the poem' as an arguable claim. Sample answer: 'The poem's nature imagery steadily turns from comfort to threat, charting the speaker's loss of faith in the consoling power of the natural world.'

lessons.title: The analytical essay, rhetoric, and revision

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: You will be able to assemble your claims and evidence into a complete analytical essay, shape it with sound rhetoric, and then revise it into precise academic prose. Drafting gets your argument onto the page; revision is where the essay actually becomes good, by tightening claims, sharpening diction, and cutting what does not serve the thesis. Warm-up: think of the last thing you wrote and submitted without a second pass. Where might a reader have lost the thread? Most weak essays are not weak in ideas but in arrangement and precision, both of which revision fixes. This final lesson gives you a structure to build, a model essay to study, and a rubric to revise against, so that what you hand in argues clearly and reads cleanly from first sentence to last.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An analytical essay has a shape: an introduction that frames the text and lands a clear thesis; body paragraphs that each advance one claim with embedded evidence and analysis, ordered so each builds on the last; and a conclusion that does more than repeat, extending the argument to its larger significance. Rhetoric is the art of making that argument persuasive and clear: logical arrangement, smooth transitions that signal how ideas connect, and a controlled, credible voice. Revision is a separate, deliberate stage, not mere proofreading. You revise for argument (Is the thesis arguable and proven?), for structure (Does each paragraph earn its place and follow from the one before?), and for style (Are sentences precise, verbs strong, quotations embedded, wordiness cut?). Academic prose values exactness over flourish: the right word, the clear sentence, the claim fully supported.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Here is a model introduction to study and imitate. 'In Sonnet 18, Shakespeare appears to pay a compliment, comparing his beloved to a summer's day, but the poem is less a tribute to the beloved than a claim for the power of poetry itself. Each quatrain finds the natural world wanting, too brief, too changeable, too easily dimmed, before the closing couplet turns to insist that verse alone can defeat time: 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.' This essay argues that the sonnet's real subject is poetic immortality, and that its form, a series of concessions resolved by a final reversal, stages that argument in miniature.' Notice the moves: it frames the text, names an arguable thesis, previews the evidence, and even embeds a quotation. That is the altitude and clarity your own introductions should reach.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Your task: draft a short analytical essay (introduction, two body paragraphs, conclusion) on a single claim about one public-domain work, embedding at least two quotations, then revise it once against the rubric below. A model conclusion to aim for, continuing the Sonnet 18 essay: 'The poem's confidence is finally self-fulfilling. Centuries after every summer it dismissed has faded, the beloved it preserves is still read, which means the couplet's boast has come true: the verse did outlast the season. Sonnet 18 is thus not only about love or time but about its own survival, a poem that wins the argument it makes simply by continuing to be read.' Match that: a conclusion that extends the claim to its larger significance rather than merely restating the thesis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: a conclusion that only repeats the introduction in new words, adding nothing. Mistake: treating revision as spell-checking rather than rethinking argument and structure. Mistake: wordy, vague prose ('in today's society,' 'very unique') that dilutes precise claims. Self-check rubric, mark yes to each: the introduction frames the text and states an arguable thesis; each body paragraph advances one claim with embedded evidence and analysis; transitions show how paragraphs connect; the conclusion extends rather than repeats; sentences are precise, with strong verbs and no padding; every quotation is accurate and embedded. Exit ticket: (a) Name the three things you revise for, beyond proofreading. (b) What should a conclusion do that an introduction does not? Answers: (a) argument, structure, and style. (b) Extend the argument to its larger significance, drawing out why the interpretation matters, rather than merely stating the thesis.
